subject: Animation
title: Brenda Chapman: Breaking the Glass Ceiling
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Brenda Chapman: Breaking the Glass Ceiling.

hook.text: Brenda Chapman was the first woman to direct an animated feature at a major studio when she led Brave at Pixar.

buildup.text: Chapman had already co-directed The Prince of Egypt at DreamWorks, proving her leadership ability.

discovery.text: Brave told a story about a mother-daughter relationship — a theme Chapman drew from her own family life.

twist.text: Pixar replaced Chapman as director midway through production. Mark Andrews finished the film.

climax.text: Chapman shared the Oscar for Brave, but her removal highlighted the gender struggles women face in animation.

punchline.text: She won the Oscar for a film she was fired from directing.

quiz.question: Why was Brenda Chapman's work on Brave significant?
options: She invented the 3D rendering used in the film
She was the first woman to direct an animated feature at a major studio, despite being replaced mid-production

details.summary: Brenda Chapman was the first woman to direct a major animated feature from a top studio when she created Brave at Pixar. She also co-directed The Prince of Egypt at DreamWorks, breaking barriers in an industry long dominated by men.
details.whyItMatters: Chapman's career highlights both progress and persistent challenges for women in animation leadership. Her removal from Brave's director role during production underscored the gender dynamics that still shape the industry.
takeaways: Chapman was the first woman to direct a major studio animated feature
She co-directed The Prince of Egypt and created the story for Brave
Her career highlights ongoing gender inequality in animation leadership

faq.question: What happened with Brenda Chapman and Brave?
faq.answer: Chapman created Brave's story inspired by her relationship with her daughter. During production, Pixar replaced her as director with Mark Andrews, though she retained co-director credit. The film won the Oscar, and Chapman's experience sparked industry-wide conversations about women directors.

faq.question: How has representation of women in animation directing changed?
faq.answer: Progress has been slow. Jennifer Yuh Nelson directed Kung Fu Panda 2, and Domee Shi directed Turning Red, but women remain dramatically underrepresented as directors of major animated features. Chapman's experience remains relevant to ongoing industry conversations.
